name: Price-Momentum
outlook: Long winners, short losers based on past cumulative returns
short_description: Buy stocks with the highest past returns (winners) and sell stocks with the lowest past returns (losers) to exploit the tendency of performance to persist over medium horizons.
full_description: Price-momentum is one of the most studied anomalies in financial markets. The strategy ranks all stocks by their cumulative returns over a formation period T (typically 12 months) while skipping the most recent S months (typically 1 month) to avoid short-term reversal effects. Stocks in the top decile are purchased (the winners portfolio) and stocks in the bottom decile are sold short (the losers portfolio), creating a zero-cost long/short portfolio. The skip month is critical because very short-term returns tend to exhibit mean-reversion rather than momentum. Empirical evidence going back to Jegadeesh and Titman (1993) shows that this strategy has produced significant abnormal returns across global equity markets, though it is subject to occasional severe crashes, particularly during market recoveries after crises.
max_profit: Unlimited on long side; gains on short side limited to 100% of shorted value
max_loss: Unlimited on short side; full investment on long side
breakeven: Strategy is profitable when the spread between winner and loser portfolio returns exceeds transaction costs

name: Earnings-Momentum
outlook: Long stocks with positive earnings surprises, short stocks with negative surprises
short_description: Trade based on Standardized Unexpected Earnings (SUE), buying stocks with the most positive earnings surprises and selling those with the most negative surprises.
full_description: Earnings-momentum exploits the well-documented Post-Earnings Announcement Drift (PEAD), whereby stocks that report unexpectedly high earnings tend to continue drifting upward, and those reporting disappointingly low earnings tend to drift downward. The strategy computes the Standardized Unexpected Earnings (SUE) for each stock by taking the difference between actual earnings and expected earnings, then normalizing by the standard deviation of past earnings surprises. Stocks are ranked by SUE and sorted into decile portfolios; the strategy goes long the top SUE decile and short the bottom SUE decile. The holding period is typically around 6 months to capture the full drift. This strategy has been consistently profitable in academic studies and is distinct from price-momentum, as the two signals are largely uncorrelated and can be combined for improved performance.
max_profit: Unlimited on long side; short side gains capped at 100% of shorted value
max_loss: Unlimited on short side; full investment on long side
breakeven: Profitable when the SUE-sorted portfolio spread exceeds transaction costs over the holding period

name: Value
outlook: Long undervalued stocks with high book-to-price, short overvalued stocks with low book-to-price
short_description: Select stocks based on their Book-to-Price (B/P) ratio, buying the cheapest decile and selling the most expensive decile to capture the well-known value premium.
full_description: The value strategy is rooted in the empirical observation that stocks with high book-to-price (B/P) ratios — so-called value stocks — tend to outperform stocks with low B/P ratios — growth stocks — over time. This value premium was famously documented by Fama and French (1992) and is one of the foundational factors in asset pricing. The strategy ranks all stocks by their B/P ratio, goes long the top decile (cheapest stocks relative to book value), and shorts the bottom decile (most expensive). The holding period typically ranges from 1 to 6 months. While B/P is the most common value metric, alternatives such as earnings-to-price, cash-flow-to-price, or dividend yield can also be used. The value premium tends to be persistent across markets and time periods, though it has experienced extended periods of underperformance, particularly during growth-dominated markets.

formulas.book_to_price: \frac{B}{P} = \frac{\text{Book Value per Share}}{\text{Market Price per Share}}

max_profit: Unlimited on long side; short side gains capped at 100%
max_loss: Unlimited on short side; full investment on long side
breakeven: Profitable when value spread (high B/P minus low B/P returns) exceeds transaction costs

name: Low-Volatility Anomaly
outlook: Long low-volatility stocks, short high-volatility stocks
short_description: Exploit the anomaly that low-volatility stocks tend to deliver higher risk-adjusted returns than high-volatility stocks, contradicting the traditional risk-return tradeoff.
full_description: The low-volatility anomaly is one of the most puzzling findings in empirical finance: stocks with lower historical volatility tend to produce equal or higher returns than high-volatility stocks, directly contradicting the capital asset pricing model (CAPM) which predicts that higher risk should be compensated with higher expected returns. The strategy estimates the volatility of each stock using the standard deviation of daily or monthly returns over a lookback window, then ranks stocks by volatility. The portfolio goes long the bottom decile (lowest volatility) and shorts the top decile (highest volatility). This anomaly has been attributed to various behavioral and institutional factors, including leverage constraints, lottery preferences among investors, and benchmarking effects that cause fund managers to overweight risky stocks. The strategy tends to have lower turnover and drawdowns compared to momentum strategies, making it attractive for risk-conscious investors.
max_profit: Unlimited on long side; short side gains capped at 100%
max_loss: Unlimited on short side; full investment on long side
breakeven: Profitable when low-vol portfolio risk-adjusted returns exceed high-vol portfolio returns net of costs

name: Implied Volatility
outlook: Long stocks with rising call implied volatility, short stocks with rising put implied volatility
short_description: Trade stocks based on changes in their options' implied volatility, exploiting the information content embedded in the options market about future stock price movements.
full_description: This strategy leverages the informational advantage of the options market by examining changes in implied volatility (IV) of equity options to predict future stock returns. Empirical research shows that stocks experiencing the largest increases in call option implied volatility tend to have higher subsequent returns, while stocks with the largest increases in put option implied volatility tend to underperform. This reflects the fact that informed traders — who possess private information about a stock's future direction — often choose to trade in the options market due to its inherent leverage and anonymity. The strategy ranks stocks by the change in their call IV (or put IV) over a recent window, going long the top decile of call IV increases and shorting the top decile of put IV increases. The signal is distinct from historical volatility and captures forward-looking information that is not embedded in prices or standard factor models.
max_profit: Unlimited on long side; short side gains capped at 100%
max_loss: Unlimited on short side; full investment on long side
breakeven: Profitable when IV-sorted spread returns exceed transaction costs and borrowing fees

name: Multifactor Portfolio
outlook: Long stocks ranking highly across multiple factors, short those ranking poorly
short_description: Combine multiple alpha signals (momentum, value, volatility, etc.) into a single composite score to construct more robust and diversified portfolios.
full_description: The multifactor portfolio strategy combines F > 1 individual factor signals — such as momentum, value, low-volatility, and quality — into a single composite ranking or score for each stock. This diversification across signals reduces the risk of any single factor underperforming and tends to produce more stable returns over time. The simplest approach assigns uniform weights to each factor: the composite score for stock i is the average of its demeaned ranks across all factors, s_i = (1/F) * sum(s_{A,i}) for factors A = 1 to F. More sophisticated approaches use volatility-adjusted weights w_A that account for differences in factor volatility or historical Sharpe ratios. Stocks are then sorted by their composite score, going long the top decile and short the bottom decile. The benefit of multifactor construction is that factor returns tend to have low correlations with each other, so the combined portfolio achieves a higher Sharpe ratio than any individual factor alone.
max_profit: Unlimited on long side; short side gains capped at 100%
max_loss: Unlimited on short side; full investment on long side
breakeven: Profitable when the composite factor spread exceeds total transaction costs across rebalancing periods

name: Residual Momentum
outlook: Long stocks with high residual returns after factor adjustment, short those with low residuals
short_description: Apply momentum to stock-specific (residual) returns after removing exposure to common risk factors via Fama-French regression, resulting in a purer and more robust momentum signal.
full_description: Residual momentum refines the classic price-momentum strategy by first removing the component of stock returns attributable to common risk factors. For each stock, a time-series regression is run over a 36-month window using the Fama-French 3-factor model (market, size, and value factors). The residuals from this regression represent the stock-specific or idiosyncratic component of returns. These residuals are then cumulated over a 12-month formation period (skipping the most recent month), and stocks are ranked by their cumulative residual return. The strategy goes long the top decile and short the bottom decile of residual momentum. Research by Blitz, Huij, and Martens (2011) demonstrates that residual momentum is stronger, more persistent, and less prone to the severe crashes that plague traditional price-momentum. Because it strips out factor exposures, the resulting portfolio has near-zero loadings on market, size, and value factors, making it a cleaner alpha source.
max_profit: Unlimited on long side; short side gains capped at 100%
max_loss: Unlimited on short side; full investment on long side
breakeven: Profitable when residual-momentum spread exceeds transaction costs; lower crash risk than raw momentum

name: Pairs Trading
outlook: Dollar-neutral; exploit temporary divergence between two historically correlated stocks
short_description: Identify pairs of historically correlated stocks and trade their spread when it diverges, profiting when it mean-reverts to its historical equilibrium.
full_description: Pairs trading is a classic market-neutral strategy that identifies two stocks (A and B) with a historically stable long-run relationship — typically stocks in the same industry or with similar fundamental characteristics. The spread is defined as the log price ratio S_t = ln(P_A(t) / P_B(t)), which should be stationary if the pair is cointegrated. When the spread deviates significantly from its historical mean (measured by the z-score exceeding a threshold, typically 1.5-2.0 standard deviations), the strategy enters a trade: short the relatively expensive stock and buy the relatively cheap stock. The position is closed when the spread reverts to its mean. Because the strategy holds a long and a short position of approximately equal dollar value, it is dollar-neutral and largely insensitive to broad market movements. Risk management is critical, as pairs can permanently diverge due to structural changes such as mergers, bankruptcies, or fundamental shifts in business models.
max_profit: Limited to the convergence of the spread back to its mean
max_loss: Potentially large if the pair permanently diverges; typically managed with stop-losses
breakeven: Profitable when spread convergence gains exceed transaction costs and borrowing fees

name: Mean-Reversion Single Cluster
outlook: Dollar-neutral; overweight underperformers and underweight outperformers within a cluster
short_description: Within a cluster of correlated stocks, take contrarian positions by buying recent underperformers and selling recent outperformers relative to the cluster average.
full_description: This strategy generalizes pairs trading to a group (cluster) of N correlated stocks. A market index for the cluster is computed as the equally-weighted average return R_m = (1/N) * sum(R_i). Each stock's weight in the portfolio is then set proportional to how much it underperformed or outperformed the cluster index: w_i = -gamma * (R_i - R_m), where gamma is a scaling parameter that controls position sizing. Stocks that underperformed the cluster receive positive weights (buy), while outperformers receive negative weights (sell). By construction, the weights sum to zero, making the portfolio dollar-neutral. This mean-reversion approach works best when the stocks in the cluster share a common factor (e.g., same sector or industry) that drives their co-movement, and temporary deviations from the group are expected to correct. The strategy requires careful cluster selection and monitoring for structural breaks.
max_profit: Limited to the degree of mean-reversion within the cluster
max_loss: Potentially large if cluster structure breaks down or stocks diverge permanently
breakeven: Profitable when intra-cluster mean-reversion exceeds transaction costs

name: Mean-Reversion Multiple Clusters
outlook: Dollar-neutral across multiple clusters; exploit mean-reversion within each group
short_description: Extend single-cluster mean-reversion to multiple groups of stocks identified via clustering algorithms like k-means, running a mean-reversion strategy within each cluster.
full_description: This strategy extends the single-cluster mean-reversion approach by partitioning the entire stock universe into K clusters using unsupervised learning methods such as k-means clustering, hierarchical clustering, or correlation-based grouping. Each cluster ideally captures a group of stocks driven by a shared latent factor. Within each cluster k, a separate mean-reversion portfolio is constructed using the same methodology as the single-cluster case: compute the cluster index, then set weights proportional to deviations from the index. The total portfolio is the combination of all K cluster-level portfolios, which can be weighted equally or by cluster-specific parameters such as historical mean-reversion speed or Sharpe ratio. This multi-cluster approach offers greater diversification and can capture cross-sectional mean-reversion patterns that a single cluster would miss. However, the clustering step introduces additional complexity and the risk of unstable cluster assignments over time.
max_profit: Limited to the aggregate mean-reversion across all clusters
max_loss: Potentially large if cluster assignments are unstable or multiple clusters diverge simultaneously
breakeven: Profitable when aggregate cross-cluster mean-reversion exceeds transaction costs and clustering overhead

name: Mean-Reversion Weighted Regression
outlook: Dollar-neutral; trade deviations from a regression-estimated equilibrium
short_description: Use weighted regression to estimate the equilibrium relationship among a group of stocks, then trade deviations from the fitted values to capture mean-reversion.
full_description: This advanced mean-reversion strategy replaces the simple equally-weighted cluster index with a more sophisticated equilibrium estimate derived from weighted regression. Rather than assuming each stock contributes equally to the group average, a regression model is fitted where one stock's price (or return) is explained by a weighted combination of the other stocks in the group. The weights in the regression can reflect factors such as market capitalization, liquidity, or historical correlation strength. Deviations of actual prices from the regression-fitted values represent the trading signal: large positive residuals indicate the stock is expensive relative to its peers (short signal), while large negative residuals indicate it is cheap (buy signal). This approach can also incorporate cointegration testing to ensure the regression residuals are stationary, providing a more rigorous statistical foundation than simple correlation-based pair or cluster trading. The complexity of model estimation and the need for rolling recalibration make this an advanced strategy.
max_profit: Limited to the magnitude of equilibrium deviations and their subsequent correction
max_loss: Potentially large if the regression relationship breaks down or regime changes occur
breakeven: Profitable when regression-estimated mean-reversion exceeds transaction costs and model estimation error

name: Single Moving Average
outlook: Trend-following; long when price is above the moving average, flat or short when below
short_description: Buy when the stock price crosses above its simple moving average and sell when it crosses below, using the moving average as a trend filter.
full_description: The single moving average strategy is one of the simplest and most widely used technical trading rules. It computes a simple moving average (SMA) of the stock's closing price over T periods (commonly T = 50 or T = 200 days). A buy signal is generated when the current price crosses above the moving average from below, indicating the beginning of an uptrend. A sell signal is generated when the price crosses below the moving average, indicating a potential downtrend. The choice of T controls the sensitivity of the strategy: shorter windows produce more frequent signals and capture trends earlier but generate more false signals (whipsaws), while longer windows produce fewer but more reliable signals at the cost of late entries. Despite its simplicity, this strategy has been shown to add value as a risk management tool, particularly by keeping investors out of major market downturns.
max_profit: Unlimited when following an extended trend
max_loss: Limited to whipsaw losses during range-bound markets plus transaction costs
breakeven: Profitable when trend-following gains exceed losses from false signals and trading costs

name: Two Moving Averages
outlook: Trend-following; long on golden cross, flat or short on death cross
short_description: Use two moving averages of different lengths and trade the crossover signals — buy on a golden cross (short MA crosses above long MA) and sell on a death cross (short MA crosses below).
full_description: The two moving average crossover strategy improves upon the single moving average by using two SMAs with different lookback periods — a shorter one (e.g., 50-day) and a longer one (e.g., 200-day). A buy signal, known as a 'golden cross,' is generated when the short-term MA crosses above the long-term MA, suggesting that recent price momentum is turning positive relative to the longer-term trend. A sell signal, known as a 'death cross,' occurs when the short-term MA crosses below the long-term MA. By comparing two averages rather than price to a single average, this approach filters out more noise and reduces the frequency of whipsaw trades in sideways markets. Common parameter combinations include 10/50, 20/100, and 50/200 day pairs. The strategy works best in strongly trending markets and underperforms in choppy, range-bound conditions where the moving averages repeatedly cross each other.
max_profit: Unlimited when capturing a sustained trend
max_loss: Limited to accumulated whipsaw losses during trendless periods
breakeven: Profitable when trending periods are long enough to offset losses during non-trending periods

name: Three Moving Averages
outlook: Trend-following with confirmation; long when short > medium > long MA alignment holds
short_description: Use short, medium, and long-term moving averages together to confirm trend direction and filter out false signals before entering positions.
full_description: The three moving average strategy adds a third layer of confirmation to the moving average crossover approach. It uses three SMAs — short-term (e.g., 10-day), medium-term (e.g., 50-day), and long-term (e.g., 200-day). A strong buy signal is generated when the short MA is above the medium MA, which is in turn above the long MA (short > medium > long), confirming a well-established uptrend across multiple time horizons. Conversely, a sell signal requires the reverse ordering (short < medium < long). Partial alignments can be used for position sizing: full position when all three align, half position when only two align. This multi-timeframe confirmation significantly reduces the number of false signals compared to single or dual moving average systems, at the cost of later entries and exits. The strategy is particularly effective in markets with strong secular trends and is commonly used in conjunction with other technical indicators for additional filtering.
max_profit: Unlimited during strong sustained trends
max_loss: Limited to losses from delayed entries/exits and whipsaws during transitions
breakeven: Profitable when confirmation-filtered trends outweigh the cost of delayed entries and missed short-term moves

name: Support and Resistance
outlook: Range-bound; buy near support levels, sell near resistance levels
short_description: Identify historical support (price floor) and resistance (price ceiling) levels from past price action, buying near support and selling near resistance.
full_description: Support and resistance trading is a foundational technical analysis strategy built on the observation that prices tend to reverse at certain key levels where buying or selling pressure has historically concentrated. Support levels are prices at which a stock has repeatedly bounced upward, reflecting strong buyer interest. Resistance levels are prices at which a stock has repeatedly reversed downward, reflecting strong seller interest or profit-taking. The strategy buys when the price approaches a support level (expecting a bounce) and sells when it approaches a resistance level (expecting a reversal). Support and resistance levels can be identified from prior highs and lows, round numbers, volume-weighted price clusters, or pivot points. A breakout above resistance can flip that level into new support, and vice versa. Risk management typically involves placing stop-loss orders just below support (for longs) or just above resistance (for shorts) to limit losses if the level fails to hold.
max_profit: Limited to the range between support and resistance (for range-bound trades); unlimited for breakout trades
max_loss: Limited by stop-loss placement below support or above resistance
breakeven: Profitable when the frequency of successful bounces at support/resistance exceeds the cost of stop-outs on failed levels

name: Channel
outlook: Range-bound or trend-following; trade within defined price channels
short_description: Define upper and lower price channels (e.g., Donchian channels or Bollinger Bands) and trade reversals at the boundaries or breakouts beyond them.
full_description: Channel trading strategies define a price envelope around a stock using upper and lower bounds, then trade based on the price's interaction with these boundaries. Common channel types include Donchian channels (highest high and lowest low over N periods), Bollinger Bands (moving average plus/minus K standard deviations), and Keltner channels (moving average plus/minus a multiple of the Average True Range). In range-bound markets, the strategy buys at the lower channel boundary and sells at the upper boundary, effectively trading the mean-reversion within the channel. In trending markets, a breakout above the upper boundary can signal a long entry, while a breakdown below the lower boundary signals a short entry. The channel width provides a dynamic measure of volatility, with wider channels indicating higher volatility and narrower channels suggesting potential breakout setups. Position sizing can be adjusted based on channel width, with tighter stops in narrow channels.
max_profit: Limited to channel width for range trades; unlimited for breakout trades in trending markets
max_loss: Limited by stop-loss; typically one channel width for failed breakouts
breakeven: Profitable when channel-based entries produce sufficient gains to offset false breakouts and trading costs

name: Event-Driven M&A
outlook: Long target company, short acquirer in stock-financed deals; profit from deal spread convergence
short_description: Trade around merger and acquisition announcements by going long the target company and shorting the acquirer (in stock deals) to profit from the deal spread narrowing as the merger closes.
full_description: Event-driven M&A (merger arbitrage) is a strategy that seeks to profit from the price dynamics surrounding announced mergers and acquisitions. When a deal is announced, the target company's stock typically jumps toward (but remains below) the offer price, while the acquiring company's stock may decline due to dilution concerns or overpayment risk. The deal spread — the difference between the target's current price and the offer price — represents the potential profit. In stock-financed deals, the strategy goes long the target and short the acquirer in the appropriate exchange ratio, creating a hedge against market-wide movements. The primary risk is deal failure, which can cause the target's price to collapse back to pre-announcement levels. Successful merger arbitrage requires deep fundamental analysis of the deal's likelihood of completion, including regulatory hurdles, financing conditions, shareholder approval, and antitrust considerations. Risk management through position sizing and diversification across multiple deals is essential.
max_profit: Limited to the deal spread (typically 3-15% annualized per deal)
max_loss: Large if the deal fails; target price can fall 20-40% or more back to pre-announcement levels
breakeven: Profitable when the probability-weighted deal spread exceeds the expected loss from deal failures

name: Machine Learning KNN
outlook: Data-driven; trade signals generated by k-nearest neighbor classification on technical features
short_description: Apply k-nearest neighbor (KNN) classification to technical features of individual stocks to generate buy/sell signals based on historically similar market patterns.
full_description: This strategy applies the k-nearest neighbor (KNN) machine learning algorithm to generate single-stock trading signals. For each stock, a feature vector is constructed from technical indicators such as moving average ratios, RSI, momentum, volatility, and volume metrics. The algorithm stores historical feature-label pairs, where labels indicate the subsequent return direction (up or down). When a new prediction is needed, KNN finds the k most similar historical observations in feature space (using Euclidean or other distance metrics) and predicts the return direction based on a majority vote among the k neighbors. Buy signals are generated when the prediction is positive; sell signals when negative. The choice of k, the feature set, and the distance metric are hyperparameters that require careful tuning, typically via cross-validation on out-of-sample data. KNN has the advantage of being non-parametric and making no distributional assumptions about returns, but it suffers from the curse of dimensionality and can be computationally expensive with large datasets.
max_profit: Unlimited on long side; short side gains capped at 100%
max_loss: Unlimited on short side; full investment on long side; model risk adds additional loss potential
breakeven: Profitable when classification accuracy exceeds the breakeven accuracy implied by the payoff ratio and transaction costs

name: Statistical Arbitrage Optimization
outlook: Dollar-neutral; systematically exploit mispricings via mean-variance optimized portfolios
short_description: Use mean-variance optimization with a covariance matrix to construct dollar-neutral portfolios that maximize expected return per unit of risk from cross-sectional stock mispricings.
full_description: Statistical arbitrage optimization constructs portfolios using a formal mean-variance optimization framework. The portfolio weights are determined by solving w = gamma * C^(-1) * E, where C is the estimated covariance matrix of stock returns, E is the vector of expected excess returns (alphas), and gamma is a risk-aversion parameter. The resulting weights naturally tilt toward stocks with high expected returns and low covariance with each other. A dollar-neutral constraint (sum of weights equals zero) is imposed to ensure market neutrality. The covariance matrix can be estimated using historical returns, factor models, or shrinkage estimators to improve stability. The expected return vector is typically derived from quantitative signals such as factor scores, momentum, or machine learning predictions. This approach provides a theoretically optimal way to combine multiple signals while controlling portfolio risk, but it is sensitive to estimation errors in both the covariance matrix and expected returns. Regularization techniques and portfolio constraints are often necessary to prevent extreme positions.
max_profit: Dependent on the magnitude of mispricings and portfolio leverage
max_loss: Potentially large during periods of factor crowding or correlation breakdowns; managed via risk limits
breakeven: Profitable when alpha signals are accurate enough to overcome estimation error and transaction costs

name: Market-Making
outlook: Neutral; profit from the bid-ask spread while managing inventory risk
short_description: Provide liquidity by continuously posting bid and ask quotes, profiting from the spread between buy and sell prices while managing the risk of holding inventory.
full_description: Market-making is a liquidity provision strategy where the trader posts simultaneous bid (buy) and ask (sell) quotes in a stock, profiting from the difference — the bid-ask spread. The market maker earns the spread each time they buy at the bid and sell at the ask. However, the strategy carries significant inventory risk: if the stock price moves adversely while the market maker holds a position, the losses can exceed the spread income. Sophisticated market-making models, such as the Avellaneda-Stoikov framework, dynamically adjust quotes based on current inventory levels, volatility, and order flow imbalances. When inventory is long (too much stock), the bid price is lowered and the ask is made more aggressive to encourage selling; when short, the opposite adjustment is made. The strategy requires low-latency execution infrastructure, tight risk controls, and sophisticated models for estimating fair value in real time. Modern market-making is dominated by high-frequency trading firms with advanced technology.

formulas.reservation_price: r(s, q, t) = s - q \cdot \gamma \cdot \sigma^2 \cdot (T - t)

max_profit: Accumulated bid-ask spread over many trades; limited per-trade profit
max_loss: Potentially large from adverse inventory exposure during volatile markets or information events
breakeven: Profitable when average spread earned exceeds adverse selection costs and inventory holding losses

name: Alpha Combos
outlook: Neutral or directional; combine multiple alpha signals for a more robust composite prediction
short_description: Combine multiple alpha signals — such as momentum, value, and sentiment — using weighted averaging or optimization to produce a more robust and diversified composite trading signal.
full_description: Alpha combination is a meta-strategy that takes multiple individual alpha signals and blends them into a single composite signal that is more robust and has a higher Sharpe ratio than any individual component. Each alpha signal a_j provides a cross-sectional prediction of expected stock returns. The composite alpha for stock i is computed as alpha_i = sum(w_j * a_{j,i}), where w_j are the combination weights. Weights can be set using several approaches: equal weighting for simplicity, inverse-variance weighting for risk parity across signals, or full mean-variance optimization using the covariance matrix of alpha returns. More advanced methods use machine learning (e.g., ridge regression, elastic net, or gradient boosting) to learn optimal combination weights from historical data. The key challenge is avoiding overfitting, especially when the number of alpha signals is large relative to the available historical data. Regularization, out-of-sample testing, and signal decay analysis are essential components of a robust alpha combination framework.
max_profit: Dependent on the combined strength of the underlying alpha signals and portfolio leverage
max_loss: Potentially large during periods when multiple signals fail simultaneously; managed via diversification and risk limits
breakeven: Profitable when the combined alpha net of transaction costs and signal decay exceeds zero
